g.text: 215,000 orders/sec is modest. Tens of microseconds at p99.99 is not.
Most systems optimize the average and monitor the tail. An exchange treats the TAIL AS THE PRODUCT.
The whole product: buyers and sellers meeting at a price
A match produces TWO executions (fills) - one per side. And the execution price is the RESTING
order's price, not the incoming one's: a resting sell at 415.00 meeting a buy willing to pay
420.00 trades at 415.00. The resting order established the price and holds time priority;
the aggressor takes what is offered. Using the incoming price would overcharge every
The budget, and what it eliminates
Read down that column and the architecture writes itself. ONE same-rack hop
consumes the entire budget; a same-datacentre hop exceeds it by an order of
magnitude. So anything involving a network or a disk is excluded from the
critical path - not as an optimization, but because a single instance of it
exceeds the whole envelope. What survives: memory, and shared memory.
Every property people care about is about TIME
a trading strategy's profitability is a
function of how fast it can react. A 100us
a LATENCY property in disguise: if two
subscribers get the same update at measurably
different times, the earlier one can trade
against the later one's stale view.
two parties whose orders crossed must agree,
afterwards and forever, on exactly what
happened and in what order - and after a crash
the exchange must reconstruct the IDENTICAL
Fairness is not a nicety - with unicast to 300 subscribers, whoever is early in your iteration order can extract money from
whoever is late, based on an implementation detail nobody agreed to. In most jurisdictions that is the VENUE's problem.
Not a large number - the message queue in this
guide handles twice that PER NODE. Nobody needs
to shard for capacity, and volume splits cleanly
So: this is not a throughput design, it is a LATENCY design - and that reframe is the most useful thing to establish early.
